claim: TET21N neuroblastoma cells were imaged and tracked for up to ten generations during exponential growth.
source: To study how far intra-generational cell-cycle correlations extend within cell pedigrees, we generated extensive lineage trees by imaging and tracking TET21N neuroblastoma cells for up to ten generations during exponential growth (Figure 1A, Figure 1—video 1, Figure 1—source data 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental procedure of imaging and tracking cells, which is a direct observation.

claim: Autonomous cycling of TET21N cells is controlled by ectopic expression of the MYC-family oncogene MYCN.
source: Autonomous cycling of these cells is controlled by ectopic expression of the MYC-family oncogene MYCN, overcoming the restriction point and thus mimicking the presence of mitogenic stimuli (Ryl et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ryl et al., 2017.

claim: High MYCN downregulated circadian clock genes in TET21N cells.
source: High MYCN also downregulated circadian clock genes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The distribution of cycle lengths was constant throughout the experiment.
source: The distribution of cycle lengths (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) was constant throughout the experiment (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) and similar across lineages (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), showing absence of experimental drift and of strong founder cell effects, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in multiple figures (1B, 1C, and supplements).

claim: The distribution of cycle lengths was similar across lineages, showing absence of strong founder cell effects.
source: The distribution of cycle lengths (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) was constant throughout the experiment (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) and similar across lineages (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), showing absence of experimental drift and of strong founder cell effects, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Lineage trees were truncated after the last generation completed by the vast majority (>95%) of lineages to avoid censoring bias.
source: To determine cycle-length correlations without censoring bias caused by finite observation time (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A; Sandler et al., 2015), we truncated all trees after the last generation completed by the vast majority (>95%) of lineages.
evidence: This is a methodological decision supported by citation to Sandler et al., 2015 and data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The resulting lineage trees were 5–7 generations deep.
source: The resulting trees were 5–7 generations deep, enabling us to reliably calculate Spearman rank correlations between relatives up to second cousins (Figure 1D,E and Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental data.

claim: Cycle-length correlations of cells with their ancestors decreased rapidly with each generation.
source: Cycle-length correlations of cells with their ancestors decreased rapidly with each generation (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The correlations increased when moving down from ancestors along side-branches—from the grandmother toward the first cousins and also from the great-grandmother toward the second cousins.
source: However, the correlations increased again when moving down from ancestors along side-branches—from the grandmother toward the first cousins and also from the great-grandmother toward the second cousins (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The actually observed cousin correlations are much larger than expected from simple inheritance of cell-cycle length alone.
source: The actually observed cousin correlations are much larger, confirming previous observations on first cousins as summarized in Sandler et al. (2015) and extending them to second cousins.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of data to theoretical expectations and citation to Sandler et al., 2015.

claim: The discrepancy between simple theoretical expectation and experimental data was not due to spatial inhomogeneity or temporal drift in the data.
source: This discrepancy between simple theoretical expectation and experimental data was not due to spatial inhomogeneity or temporal drift in the data (Figure 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 3C-E).
evidence: This is supported by control analyses shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3C-E.

claim: The lineage trees show long-ranging intra-generational correlations that cannot be explained by the inheritance of cell-cycle length.
source: Thus, the lineage trees show long-ranging intra-generational correlations that cannot be explained by the inheritance of cell-cycle length.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of observed data to theoretical expectations.

claim: More than one heritable factor is required to generate the observed cell-cycle correlations in T cell lineage trees.
source: Theoretical work has shown that more than one heritable factor is required to generate the observed cell-cycle correlations in T cell lineage trees, while the nature of these heritable factors has remained unclear (Markham et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Markham et al., 2010.

claim: High intra-generational correlations in the face of weak ancestral correlations have been observed in cells as diverse as bacteria, cyanobacteria, lymphocytes and mammalian cancer cells.
source: High intra-generational correlations in the face of weak ancestral correlations have been observed in cells as diverse as bacteria (Powell, 1958), cyanobacteria (Yang et al., 2010), lymphocytes (Markham et al., 2010) and mammalian cancer cells (Staudte et al., 1984; Sandler et al., 2015; Chakrabarti et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The ubiquity of the puzzling phenomenon of high intra-generational correlations suggests that it may help reveal basic principles that control cell-cycle duration.
source: The ubiquity of this puzzling phenomenon suggests that it may help reveal basic principles that control cell-cycle duration.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observed ubiquity of the phenomenon.

claim: In proliferating mammalian cells in culture, the circadian clock has been found to be entrained by the cell cycle.
source: However, in proliferating mammalian cells in culture, the circadian clock has been found to be entrained by the cell cycle (Bieler et al., 2014; Feillet et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bieler et al., 2014 and Feillet et al., 2014.

claim: The circadian clock is strongly damped or even abrogated by oncogenes such as MYC.
source: Moreover, the circadian clock is strongly damped or even abrogated by oncogenes such as MYC (Altman et al., 2015; Shostak et al., 2016) yet MYC-driven cancer cells retain high intra-generational correlations (Ryl et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Altman et al., 2015 and Shostak et al., 2016.

claim: MYC-driven cancer cells retain high intra-generational correlations despite circadian clock disruption.
source: Moreover, the circadian clock is strongly damped or even abrogated by oncogenes such as MYC (Altman et al., 2015; Shostak et al., 2016) yet MYC-driven cancer cells retain high intra-generational correlations (Ryl et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ryl et al., 2017.

claim: A minimal requirement for maintaining cell size is that cells reach a critical size before dividing, which can be achieved by delaying S phase.
source: A minimal requirement for maintaining cell size is that cells reach a critical size before dividing, which can be achieved by delaying S phase (Shields et al., 1978).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Shields et al., 1978.

claim: The simplest model that generated high intra-generational correlations was based on the independent inheritance of two latent variables (Model III).
source: The simplest model that generated high intra-generational correlations was based on the independent inheritance of two latent variables (Model III; Figure 2C, cyan dots), whereas one-variable models failed to meet this criterion (Model II, Figure 2C, blue dots and Model I).
evidence: This is supported by model comparison shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Model III consistently overestimated ancestral correlations and hence its relative evidence was low (<10% for all data sets).
source: However, Model III consistently overestimated ancestral correlations and hence its relative evidence was low (<10% for all data sets).
evidence: This is based on Bayesian model comparison using the experimental data.

claim: In Model V, both latent variables had long-ranging memories, with ∼50% decay over 2–3 generations.
source: Model V produced a remarkable inheritance pattern (Figure 2D): Individually, both latent variables had long-ranging memories, with ∼50% decay over 2–3 generations.
evidence: This is based on analysis of Model V shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The negative unidirectional coupling in Model V cross-correlated the variables negatively along an ancestral line, resulting in cycle-length correlations that essentially vanished after one generation.
source: However, the negative unidirectional coupling cross-correlated the variables negatively along an ancestral line, resulting in cycle-length correlations that essentially vanished after one generation.
evidence: This is based on analysis of Model V properties.

claim: The coexistence of rapidly decaying ancestral correlations and extended intra-generational correlations can be explained by the inheritance of two latent variables, one of which inhibits the other.
source: We conclude that the coexistence of rapidly decaying ancestral correlations and extended intra-generational correlations can be explained by the inheritance of two latent variables, one of which inhibits the other.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the BAR model analysis.

claim: During symmetric cell division, both cell size and regulators of cell-cycle progression are passed on from the mother to the daughter cells.
source: During symmetric cell division, both cell size and regulators of cell-cycle progression are passed on from the mother to the daughter cells (Spencer et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2017; Arora et al., 2017; Barr et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Growth and cell-cycle progression can be separately manipulated experimentally in mammalian cells.
source: Indeed, growth and cell-cycle progression can be separately manipulated experimentally in mammalian cells (Fingar et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fingar et al., 2002.

claim: Cells continue to grow in size when regulatory license is withheld, for example in the absence of mitogens, and growth is not otherwise constrained.
source: In particular, cells continue to grow in size when regulatory license is withheld, for example in the absence of mitogens, and growth is not otherwise constrained, for example by mechanical force or growth inhibitors (Fingar et al., 2002; Conlon and Raff, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fingar et al., 2002 and Conlon and Raff, 2003.

claim: If a delayed regulatory license prolongs the mother's cell cycle, it will grow large, and by size inheritance, its daughters will be large at birth, reach a size sufficient for division quickly and hence may have shorter cell cycles.
source: This interaction alone implies an effect of one inherited variable, cycle progression, on the other, cell growth, that anti-correlates subsequent cell cycles (as required by BAR model V): If a delayed regulatory license prolongs the mother's cell cycle, it will grow large. By size inheritance, its daughters will be large at birth, reach a size sufficient for division quickly and hence may have shorter cell cycles.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the consequences of the growth-progression model.

claim: The growth-progression model reproduced the cycle-length distribution and the ancestral and intra-generational correlations.
source: The parameterized model yielded a stationary cell size distribution (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) and reproduced the cycle-length distribution (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C) as well as the ancestral and intra-generational correlations (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by model fits shown in multiple figures.

claim: The dynamics of cell growth and cell-cycle progression, coupled only through a minimum-size requirement, account for the intricate cycle-length patterns in lineage trees.
source: Thus, the dynamics of cell growth and cell-cycle progression, coupled only through a minimum-size requirement, account for the intricate cycle-length patterns in lineage trees.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model fitting results.

claim: Individual cell cycles in the model are either growth-limited (division happens upon reaching the minimum size) or progression-limited (the cell grows beyond the minimum size until the cycle is completed).
source: Individual cell cycles in the model are either growth-limited, that is division happens upon reaching the minimum size, or progression-limited, that is the cell grows beyond the minimum size until the cycle is completed (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a description of the model behavior shown in figures.

claim: If both mother and daughter are progression-limited, their cycles are positively correlated.
source: If both mother and daughter are progression-limited (i.e., the threshold size is exceeded by both), their cycles are positively correlated (Figure 3E, green dots).
evidence: This is based on model simulation results shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Mother-daughter pairs that involve at least one growth limitation show near-zero or negative correlations.
source: By contrast, all mother-daughter pairs that involve at least one growth limitation show near-zero (Figure 3E, cyan dots) or negative correlations (Figure 3E, magenta and black dots).
evidence: This is based on model simulation results shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Cousin correlations are carried specifically by cousins that descend from a grandmother with a progression-limited cell cycle.
source: While cousins are positively correlated overall, this correlation is carried specifically by cousins that descend from a grandmother with a progression-limited cell cycle (Figure 3F, blue dots), whereas cousins stemming from a growth-limited grandmother are hardly correlated (Figure 3F, orange dots).
evidence: This is based on model simulation results shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Growth inhibition increased cousin correlations relative to mother-daughter correlations, whereas slowing cell-cycle progression decreased these correlations.
source: Indeed, using the model to simulate perturbation experiments (Figure 3—source data 1), we found that growth inhibition increased cousin correlations relative to mother-daughter correlations, whereas slowing cell-cycle progression decreased these correlations (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on model predictions shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Lowering MYCN slowed cell-cycle progression while allowing considerable cell growth, as evidenced by cells growing to larger average size over longer and more variable cell cycles.
source: Cells grew to larger average size (Figure 4B, blue lines) over longer and more variable cell cycles (Figure 4C). These data show that lowering MYCN slowed cell-cycle progression while allowing considerable cell growth.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: Expression of mTOR was not lowered by MYCN inhibition.
source: Further consistent with this phenotype, expression of mTOR, a central regulator of metabolism and growth (Fingar et al., 2002), was not lowered (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Rapamycin treatment reduced cell size by a small but reproducible amount.
source: In a separate experiment, we inhibited cell growth by applying the mTOR inhibitor rapamycin, which reduced cell size by a small but reproducible amount (Figure 4B, red lines).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Rapamycin treatment lengthened the cell cycle slightly without changing MYCN protein levels.
source: This treatment also lengthened the cell cycle slightly (Figure 4C) but without changing MYCN protein levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Lowering MYCN and inhibiting mTOR are orthogonal perturbations that act on cell-cycle progression and cell growth, respectively.
source: Thus, lowering MYCN and inhibiting mTOR are orthogonal perturbations that act on cell-cycle progression and cell growth, respectively.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: Lowering MYCN decreased intra-generational correlation and removed second-cousin correlations.
source: As predicted by the growth-progression model, these perturbations resulted in markedly different cycle-length correlation patterns within lineage trees (Figure 4D,E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D): Lowering MYCN decreased intra-generational correlation and, in particular, removed second-cousin correlations.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4D,E and supplements.

claim: Rapamycin treatment strongly increased intra-generational correlations and caused ancestral correlations to decline only weakly.
source: By contrast, rapamycin treatment strongly increased intra-generational correlations and caused ancestral correlations to decline only weakly.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4D,E.

claim: MYCN knockdown cells grew larger, requiring logistic regulation of growth rate at large cell sizes to obtain a stable cell-size distribution in the model.
source: MYCN knockdown cells grew larger; to obtain a stable cell-size distribution for the corresponding model fits, we implemented logistic regulation of growth rate at large cell sizes.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations and modeling requirements.

claim: The vast majority of cell cycles were progression-limited after MYCN inhibition.
source: As a result, the vast majority of cell cycles were progression-limited (Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is based on model simulation results shown in Figure 4F and supplement.

claim: Rapamycin treatment increased the fraction of growth-limited cell cycles.
source: Taken together, rapamycin treatment increased the fraction of growth-limited cell cycles (Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F) and inheritance of cell-cycle progression speed, thus causing increased ancestral and intra-generational correlations.
evidence: This is based on model simulation results shown in Figure 4F and supplement.

claim: Growth may be limiting primarily for rapidly proliferating cell types, even without specific growth inhibition.
source: We hypothesized that growth may be limiting primarily for rapidly proliferating cell types, even without specific growth inhibition.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: Mouse embryonic stem cells proliferate much faster than the neuroblastoma cells.
source: We analyzed time-lapse microscopy data of non-transformed mouse embryonic stem cells (Filipczyk et al., 2015) that proliferate much faster than the neuroblastoma cells (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on analysis of data from Filipczyk et al., 2015 shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Side-branch correlations of cycle length were large in mouse embryonic stem cells.
source: Side-branch correlations of cycle length were again large (Figure 5B Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), as seen in the previous data except for the MYCN-inhibited cells.
evidence: This is based on data analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The BAR model required two negatively coupled variables to account for the mouse embryonic stem cell data.
source: As before, the BAR model required two negatively coupled variables to account for these data (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This is based on model comparison shown in Figure 5C and supplements.

claim: The majority (∼60%) of cell cycles were limited by growth in mouse embryonic stem cells.
source: Fitting the growth-progression model to the data (Figure 5A,B), we found that the majority (∼60%) of cell cycles were limited by growth (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), indicating that cycle length of fast proliferating mammalian cells is, to a large extent, controlled by growth.
evidence: This is based on model fitting results shown in Figure 5D and supplement.

claim: Cycle length of fast proliferating mammalian cells is, to a large extent, controlled by growth.
source: Fitting the growth-progression model to the data (Figure 5A,B), we found that the majority (∼60%) of cell cycles were limited by growth (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), indicating that cycle length of fast proliferating mammalian cells is, to a large extent, controlled by growth.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model fitting results.

claim: The seemingly paradoxical pattern of cell-cycle lengths in lineage trees can be accounted for by the inheritance of two types of quantities: resources accumulated during the cell cycle (cell 'size') and regulators governing the speed of cell-cycle progression.
source: Here, we showed that the seemingly paradoxical pattern of cell-cycle lengths in lineage trees, with rapidly decaying ancestral and long-range intra-generational correlations, can be accounted for by the inheritance of two types of quantities: resources accumulated during the cell cycle (cell 'size') and regulators governing the speed of cell-cycle progression.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on all the presented data and modeling.

claim: The fact that cell size and cell-cycle progression are fundamental processes in dividing cells may help explain the ubiquity of the paradoxical cell-cycle pattern.
source: The fact that these are fundamental processes in dividing cells may help explain the ubiquity of the paradoxical cell-cycle pattern.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on the findings.

claim: Targeted experimental perturbations of cell growth and cell-cycle progression support the growth-progression model.
source: Targeted experimental perturbations of cell growth and cell-cycle progression support our model.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental perturbation results.

claim: Modulation of the cell cycle by the circadian clock has been suggested as an alternative mechanism underlying the observed cell-cycle variability and cousin correlations, with strongest experimental evidence to date for cyanobacteria.
source: As an alternative mechanism underlying the observed cell-cycle variability and cousin correlations, modulation of the cell cycle by the circadian clock has been suggested, with strongest experimental evidence to date for cyanobacteria (Sandler et al., 2015; Mosheiff et al., 2018; Py et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Unlike cyanobacteria, proliferating mammalian cells show entrainment of the circadian clock to the cell cycle with periods well below 24 hr.
source: Unlike cyanobacteria, proliferating mammalian cells show entrainment of the circadian clock to the cell cycle with periods well below 24 hr (Bieler et al., 2014; Feillet et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bieler et al., 2014 and Feillet et al., 2014.

claim: All data sets which displayed long-range correlation patterns selected a BAR model featuring long-range inheritance of two memory variables, which is masked in mother-daughter pairs by an anticorrelating interaction between them.
source: All data sets which displayed long-range correlation patterns (control replicate rep1 and rapamycin treatment of neuroblastoma cells as well as ESCs) selected a BAR model featuring long-range inheritance of two memory variables, which is masked in mother-daughter pairs by an anticorrelating interaction between them.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the Bayesian model selection analysis.

claim: Size inheritance is predicted to be particularly long-range by the fits of the growth-progression model to the experimental data.
source: Size inheritance is predicted to be particularly long-range by the fits of the growth-progression model to the experimental data.
evidence: This is based on model fitting results.

claim: Long-range memory of size emerges because growth does not force cell-cycle progression, allowing cells to grow large in progression-limited cycles and then pass on size over several generations.
source: This memory emerges because growth does not force cell-cycle progression, allowing cells to grow large in progression-limited cycles and then pass on size over several generations.
evidence: This is an explanation of the model behavior.

claim: Recent work has shown the existence of negative feedback of cell size on growth rate.
source: Recent work on this problem has shown the existence of negative feedback of cell size on growth rate (Ginzberg et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ginzberg et al., 2018.

claim: The results remain robust when implementing logistic dependence of growth rate on size in the growth-progression model.
source: We have found that our results remain robust when implementing a simple form of such a feedback (logistic dependence of growth rate on size) in the growth-progression model.
evidence: This is based on additional model analysis.

claim: Growth of many mammalian cells during the cell cycle adds a volume that only weakly increases with cell volume at birth (termed near-adder behavior).
source: Another recent study has shown that growth of many mammalian cells during the cell cycle adds a volume that only weakly increases with cell volume at birth (termed near-adder behavior, Cadart et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cadart et al., 2018.

claim: Near-adder behavior appears to be caused by a combination of growth-rate regulation and cell-size effects on cell-cycle progression.
source: This behavior appears to be caused by a combination of growth-rate regulation and cell-size effects on cell-cycle progression.
evidence: This is a statement about the interpretation of previous work.

claim: Factoring in the cell-cycle length correlations studied here will help uncover the mechanistic details of cell size regulation.
source: We expect that factoring in the cell-cycle length correlations studied here will help uncover the mechanistic details of cell size regulation.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research directions.

claim: The inference approach could be extended to include finely resolved data on cell-cycle phases as well as multiple cell fates via asymmetric division and differentiation.
source: Moreover, we envisage that our inference approach could be extended to include finely resolved data on cell-cycle phases (Chao et al., 2019) as well as multiple cell fates via asymmetric division and differentiation (Duffy et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research directions with citations.

claim: Cells of the same type growing in homogeneous conditions often have highly heterogeneous cycle lengths.
source: Cells of the same type growing in homogeneous conditions often have highly heterogeneous cycle lengths (Smith and Martin, 1973).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Smith and Martin, 1973.

claim: The minimal duration of the cell cycle will be determined by the maximal cellular growth rate in a given condition.
source: The minimal duration of the cell cycle will be determined by the maximal cellular growth rate in a given condition (Kafri et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kafri et al., 2016.

claim: Many cells, in particular in multicellular organisms, do not grow at maximum rate, and their cycle length appears to be set by the progression of regulatory machinery through a series of checkpoints.
source: However, many cells, in particular, in multicellular organisms, do not grow at maximum rate, and their cycle length appears to be set by the progression of regulatory machinery through a series of checkpoints (Novak et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Novak et al., 2007.

claim: Cycle lengths are similar in sister cells, which may be due to the inheritance of molecular regulators across mitosis.
source: Such studies across many cell types have found that cycle lengths are similar in sister cells, which may be due to the inheritance of molecular regulators across mitosis (Spencer et al., 2013; Mitchell et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2017; Barr et al., 2017; Arora et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Ancestral correlations in cycle length fade rapidly, often disappearing between grandmother and granddaughter cells, or already between mother and daughter cells.
source: By contrast, ancestral correlations in cycle length fade rapidly, often disappearing between grandmother and granddaughter cells, or already between mother and daughter cells.
evidence: This is a general observation from the literature.

claim: The cycle lengths of cousin cells are found to be correlated, indicating that the grandmothers exert concealed effects through at least two generations.
source: Remarkably, however, the cycle lengths of cousin cells are found to be correlated, indicating that the grandmothers exert concealed effects through at least two generations.
evidence: This is a general observation from the literature.

claim: Animal cells can grow very large without dividing.
source: By contrast, animal cells can grow very large without dividing (Conlon and Raff, 2003), and recent precise measurements suggest that growth control involves both modulation of growth rate and cell-cycle length (Sung et al., 2013; Tzur et al., 2009; Cadart et al., 2018; Ginzberg et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Conlon and Raff, 2003.

claim: Recent precise measurements suggest that growth control involves both modulation of growth rate and cell-cycle length.
source: By contrast, animal cells can grow very large without dividing (Conlon and Raff, 2003), and recent precise measurements suggest that growth control involves both modulation of growth rate and cell-cycle length (Sung et al., 2013; Tzur et al., 2009; Cadart et al., 2018; Ginzberg et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: PER1, CRY2, NR1D1, and PER3 are differentially expressed in TET21N cells with high versus low MYCN expression with p values < 0.05.
source: (A) Test for differential expression of circadian clock genes in TET21N cells with high versus low MYCN expression using edgeR (Robinson and Smyth, 2008), based on estimating dispersion for each gene using the negative binomial distribution. Differentially expressed genes are PER1, CRY2, NR1D1, and PER3, with p values < 0.05.
evidence: This is based on differential expression analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The circadian clock module is significantly downregulated in TET21N cells with high MYCN (p value = 0.016).
source: (B) Comparison of expression of the entire circadian clock module (via averaged fold change) with 104 randomly drawn gene modules with comparable dispersion. The circadian clock module (black dot) is significantly downregulated (p value = 0.016).
evidence: This is based on gene module analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.
